meta.title: AI is slowly munching away my passion
meta.author: dzervas

comments.author: nextos
comments.text:
In my opinion, we are currently overestimating the impact of LLMs. While they are fantastic information retrieval tools, I remain skeptical that they can reliably ship software, regardless of how much reinforcement learning is bolted onto them.

Instead, we should leverage LLMs to automate mundane tasks while utilizing theorem proving, model checking, and other formal verification techniques to truly increase software quality taking advantage of the extra productivity gains.

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
I think the impact may be bigger long term by LLMs changing how software is "shipped", or what software even is.

When the cost to write code is high, we treat it as a precious artifact. We maintain it, update it, and ship the same code to all users. The quality must be high, because bugs can affect many users and long-term maintenance.

But I think there's a chance we'll get a lot more disposable single-use software. Programs created on the fly to solve one task and then discarded. Nothing to maintain. Whether they're buggy or not is judged only by an individual user being satisfied with results on a particular task.

comments.author: agent281
comments.text:
One area I'm somewhat bullish on is internal software tools, especially when they make hidden information more consumable.

I just built a little UI for visualizing a data product. It's always been easy to throw a dashboard together, but this looked more like a frontend display. I'm hoping that it will make design conversations with product more concrete.

It's not something that should ever see the light of day though. It should just be an internal tool for maybe couple dozen people.

Why invest in good code hygiene and tech debt avoidance if you can just replace the software with a few minutes spent with Claude? comments.text:
What about the data produced and the damage done by the bugs?

Servers are "cattle" because they mostly work and they all work the same. Hordes of custom made programs, each with its own bugs, are more like pets here. I would call the direction "let's have a larger number of pets suffering from more neglect"

comments.author: zladuric
comments.text:
Uh, I think we moved beyond pets long ago. VCs and investors aren't looking for pets, they're looking for unicorns. And in the meantime they are funding hundreds of thousands of them a year. That's a lot more like cattle then pets. Not all, but most.

Even we engineers are treating them (mostly) so. We do the best practices, we stay lean and on track, and avoid doing anything except produce work.

Even well cared for products are just that, products. Lots of especially junior people buy into the "we're special" stories, but if you've been around, you know a lot of the startups are very similar in that regard.

There are also enterprise companies building software, bit those are often even more soulless.

I'm not saying it's all bleak and sad. I just want to relay my observation that, at least to me, it's all mostly driven from a business perspective. Nothing wrong about it, you can be a good shepherd and treat your sheep well, but you're not bringing them into your house like you bring your dog or a cat.

comments.text:
What seems weird about this is that software generally does something that has a lasting impact. Sure, you made a quick tool to sort through resumes but the ones you have thrown out won't come back. And somebody will or will not get hired.

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
they at least get cheaper to modify. whether it's an improvement will depend on who's steering


The current LLM tools have problems with grasping larger codebases and having a coherent global view. Their polishing is just reshuffling things, often in a slightly lossy fashion.

Change for the sake of change is easy, good-enough is achievable, but getting to perfect may end up being asymptotically difficult.

I don't think we'll have actually good polished solid codebases out of LLMs, at least not until new a model architectures change the tradeoffs.

LLMs so far are most effective at writing dumb "glue" code that puts existing components together. The more likely scenario seems to me that we'll get more splitting of code into micro libraries and lots of abstraction layers (even more than what devs roll their eyes on seeing the excess of npm).

comments.author: nonagoninf
comments.text:
I see what you mean. Some things that we are good at were part of our (professional) identity. LLMs commoditizing those areas feels like an attack on our dignity.

In that sense, we are experiencing a similar thing manual labor workers went through during mechanization, miners when mines in Western Europe were closed, etc. A large part of one's dignity is associated with the work we do and in some countries, especially where male stereotypes are still prevalent, the food one brings to the table.

I also agree with @nextos though. Software development is highly-skilled labor, so for most people it's possible to gain skills in other, less IR'y, areas where LLMs will have a hard time.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
I used to be “the guy with that automates stuff”. I used to be the one to ask for “the company VPN hack that makes it work on Arch”. [...]

Now however, AI is the thing that automates and fixes corporate VPNs on outdated distros better than I would be able to in a thousand lifetimes. It has “robbed” me of a trait - or maybe a couple of them. [...]

Your trait isn’t taken away from you but it’s given to everyone, freely, with close to no required effort/skill/planning towards it.


I'm feeling this a bit around prototyping. For most of my career rapid prototyping was my super-power: I could knock out a working illustrative demo of an idea in an hour, then take that to a meeting and use it to elevate the conversation - my experience is that having a prototype to help solidify what's possible makes conversations so much more productive, especially if you know how to frame it so that it encourages rather than discourages new ideas.

Today, Claude can knock out better prototypes than I can in just a few minutes. My special trait suddenly isn't so special any more.

So far I've been handling this by leaning into it. I can produce a dozen prototypes in the time it used to take to create his one, which means I can explore a problem space faster and in more detail. That's an amplified version of my original trait.

It does feel weird to have a specific skill that I took pride in suddenly commoditized in this way, especially when I could name dozens more similar skills that are also affected like this.

comments.author: hwayne

That often meant knowing a lot of weird languages that happened to be good at representing a problem, knowing how to quickly skim APIs, etc. AI is a 100x better than me now. It makes me more productive, but I still feel like I lost something special.

The interesting problems are typically more about thinking than writing code and if the domain is specialized enough LLMs (still) fail quite miserably.

That said, I'm pretty opinionated what Python, shell script, or Nix should look like, so I'm still often iterating on this kind of script with an LLM if it ends up being more than a one-off.

comments.author: remmelt
comments.text: Maybe the power was not in creating the scripts themselves, but in knowing where a script might come in handy in the first place. I see a lot of colleagues still who refuse to automate even the simplest set of commands. Recurring tasks take much longer, are more tedious, and fail more often. A very simple script would already take away a lot of that work, and an LLM can easily create that script with more "features" than I could in the time I should realistically invest in it.

comments.author: enobayram
comments.text:
And it's not just programming passion, because in a world where AI can successfully replace programmers, I don't think there would be many corners left for other human intellectual endeavours either.

Today, the biggest defence most professions have against AI must be the fact that they're not practiced as openly as programming and their practitioners don't use AI as much as programmers do. But if AI is to replace programmers, then it must have become smart enough to learn brand new domains by iterating on them without human input.

I think people are delusional for thinking they're staying ahead by promoting it "write tests too" or running Ralph loops. But I think it's also delusional to think you can pivot to robotics or some other engineering field. Or even to some field that involves manual work, because humanoid (and otherwise) robots seem to be advancing quite fast as well, and I'm sure they'd also accelerate exponentially when AI gets there.

Whether or not this future becomes a reality, it's already eating away passion, because I believe human passion has a lot to do with the belief that one can focus on and invest in a domain and get better over time and reap benefits. How can you believe in that for any specific domain while it's impossible to predict what corner (if any) will be left behind?

comments.author: alexandria
comments.text:
and I'm sure they'd also accelerate exponentially when AI gets there.


Why are you so sure of that? It's certainly a claim that AI-proponents have been trying to make true since well before LLMs took off, but I've certainly never seen any evidence of it outside of a bubble whereby a number of billion dollar companies shuffle the same X billion dollars to each other.


But if AI is to replace programmers, then it must have become smart enough to learn brand new domains by iterating on them without human input.


Must it have? I don't think that's the case for current generations of LLMs and I see no reason why that would suddenly become the case in the future. I can see programmers being replaced despite this, because the majority of problem domains are very simple and, even if the LLMs were to produce what would be essentially career-ending bugs (as I've seen most of this year), the hype of the bubble is still enough that people are losing out on work, and perhaps eventually people will lose faith in our profession more generally.

comments.author: susam
comments.text:
I remember how dismayed Kasparov was after losing the 1997 match to IBM's Deep Blue, although his views on Deep Blue became more balanced with time and he accepted that we had entered a new era in which computers would outperform grandmasters at chess.

Still, chess players can take comfort in the fact that chess is still played between humans. Players make their name and fame by beating other humans, because playing against computers is no longer interesting as a competition.

Many software developers would like to have similar comfort. But that comfort is harder to find, because unlike chess, building prototypes or PoCs is not seen as a sport or art-form. It is mostly seen as a utility. So while brain-coding a PoC may still be intellectually satisfying for the programmer, to most other people it only matters that the thing works. That means that programmers do not automatically get the same protected space chess players have, where the human activity itself remains valued even after machines become stronger. The activity programmers enjoy may continue but the recognition and economic value attached to it may shrink.

So I think the big adjustment software developers have to make is this: The craft will still exist and we will still enjoy doing it but the credit and value will increasingly go to those who define problems well, connect systems, make good product decisions and make technology useful in messy real-world situations. It has already been this way for a while and will only become more so as time goes by.

comments.author: intelfx
comments.text:
The craft will still exist and we will still enjoy doing it but the credit and value will increasingly go to those who define problems well, connect systems, make good product decisions and make technology useful in messy real-world situations. It has already been this way for a while and will only become more so as time goes by.


That’s the entire point, though: it’s not programming anymore, it’s product-managing. Not everyone who is good at programming also is, or _wants to be_, good at product management. Under this assumption, the craft of programming will indeed become devalued.

comments.author: munificent
comments.text:
even though your ability to memorize the syntax of program languages is completely irrelevant now.


As someone whose deepest passion and career for the past decade has been designing that syntax, it's hard to articulate how profoundly demoralizing this whole this is for me.

Who gives a shit about programming language design in a world where people don't even read the code?

Also, this concept isn't entirely without precedent or terminology: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomie

comments.author: Corbin
comments.text:
If it helps, evidence suggests that bots can't write compilers, and Rice's theorem prevents them from achieving correctness via adherence to test suites. Evidence also is that they can't design languages; we've been cleaning up slop over at the esolangs wiki and you can see for yourself how bad AI-generated languages are. We're thinking of banning such languages entirely since they are so useless, unfunny, and time-wasting.

I'm going to keep this comment in mind when designing my next round of challenges. I think I can make an even clearer contrast between bots and competent compiler engineers.

comments.author: munificent
comments.text:
For me, it's not about whether AI can do my job.

It's that the reward of my job working on a programming language comes from the human users who read and write code in that language. When I make the language easier to understand, safer, etc. I directly improve their enjoyment of their job.

But if I'm making a programming language that is primarily output and consumed by bots, all of that intrinsic reward collapses. I simply don't care if I make it easier for an AI to do whatever it does. I understand that at the end of the day a human is driving the AI and my language can make their life better, indirectly. But it's sort of like being a chef and discovering that no one eats the food I lovingly craft anymore. They just feed it to their horse and then ride the horse around town.

comments.author: agent281
comments.text: I'm very sorry to hear you say this. Your work has been very impactful. Several of my friends and I have independently worked through Crafting Interpreters. It was very kind of you to write an open and free book like that. I know it's hard to feel good about the future right now, but I appreciate the work you've done.

comments.author: munificent

I have good days. I try to remember that despite most tech-oriented social media spaces being overrun with discussion of nothing but the coming AI utopia/dystopia, most programmers are still just out there writing code like they used to (with maybe some better auto-complete) and those programmers still care about the language they use.

But compared to the excitement of the past decade and a half where it felt like programming languages were the biggest lever around to improve the lives of software engineers, my work just feels... I don't know, diminished.

I'm working through it, but societal change is hard.

comments.author: simonw

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
They are, but it's still not clear how is that supposed to be relevant.

Wargames was a case where two (all) players could agree to cooperate (in prisoner's dilemma sense). With LLMs being much more broadly available, it's beyond the point where you can get everyone to cooperate, so you can control only how you act when others are "playing" anyway. comments.author: pyj
comments.text:
I've gone through the waves of this too, and I'm optimistic for software developers.

I remember the world before Google, Wikipedia, and social media.  Technology is like alcohol, it makes you more of yourself.  AI takes you and cranks it up to 11.

A lot of us are immersed in software development, so we can see what these things can do for us.  Programming is still a technical medium of creation, problem solving, and tradeoffs.  We have a new tool to help, and we'll be doing more "engineering" than ever.  We're going to be able to push the field and our devices further than ever before, especially into domains that were too inefficient to pursue before.

comments.author: faassen
comments.text:
The problem many of us are facing is caused by AI empowering people to do things more quickly, and making things that are hard a bit easier.

The "more quickly" is boring to me as a creative person: productivity discussions, the idea that if only we can write code a lot faster we're automatically more productive. This ignores so much we should know about systems. It ignores how difficult it is to actually measure productivity in software development. It ignores that code is a liability, not an asset. And that sometimes it's actually productive to throw away code.

But "easier" is an opportunity for us. This means that non-programmers or beginning programmers can do more advanced programming. But I am also convinced it means that advanced developers leveraging these tools can do more advanced programming, and be more creative.

Yes, I feel this anxiety, but we can use these tools to level up. To become more.

comments.author: rnb37

comments.author: thangalin
comments.text:
While vibe-coding a read-only, dependency-free front-end for raw Git repositories on self-hosted or shared-hosted servers (in PHP), adding syntax highlighting for new file formats in seconds feels incredibly rewarding and liberating.

https://repo.autonoma.ca/?repo=treetrek.git&hash=de5bfc1ca83b45fb300b9d380c6e601401c3699c&name=render%2FLanguageDefinitions.php

I'd get no joy in writing those regular expressions. Providing the source files along with a prompt such as:


What are some other popular programming languages and source file formats that are missing? Add them.


And:


The Highlighter class identifies more syntaxes than are present in the LanguageDefinitions. Find the missing syntaxes and add them.


Along with cleaning up code:


Eliminate the early return (only one exit point per method). There's some code duplication going on inside the file. Can you spot it and eliminate it?


That is joyful. Seeing the code appear more quickly and more accurately than I could ever write. That is joyful. It'll be even more fun when these code monkeys can permanently learn aspects of professional-level code like, "don't violate encapsulation", "avoid insipid comments", "avoid duplicated logic," and so forth, without having to have a file full of rules.
